title: Absolute Beginner
description: A gentle on-ramp into programming. Understand what code is, learn the building blocks, write your first real program, then pick a direction.

steps.title: What programming is
steps.summary: Code is a set of precise instructions a computer follows.
steps.detail: A program is nothing more than a list of exact steps written in a language the computer understands. The computer does precisely what you say — no more, no less — so the skill you are building is the ability to break a goal into unambiguous instructions. Everything else is detail layered on top of that one idea.

steps.title: How computers run code
steps.summary: Source code becomes instructions the machine executes.
steps.detail: The code you type is text. A tool — an interpreter or a compiler — turns that text into instructions the processor can run. Interpreted languages like Python run your text line by line; compiled languages translate the whole program up front. You don't need the deep internals yet, just the mental picture: human-readable text in, machine actions out.

steps.title: Variables & data types
steps.summary: Store and label values: numbers, text, true/false.
steps.detail: A variable is a named box that holds a value. Values come in types — whole numbers, decimals, text strings, and booleans (true/false) are the ones you'll use constantly. Picking the right type and giving variables clear names is the difference between code you can read next week and code you can't.

steps.title: Control flow
steps.summary: Make decisions (if) and repeat work (loops).
steps.detail: Programs rarely run straight through. Conditionals (if/else) let your code choose a path based on data, and loops let it repeat an action over many items without copy-pasting. Master these two and you can already express most everyday logic.

steps.title: Functions
steps.summary: Package reusable logic with a name and inputs.
steps.detail: A function bundles a chunk of work behind a name, optionally taking inputs and returning a result. Functions keep programs short and readable: write the logic once, call it everywhere. Thinking in small, well-named functions is the first real step toward writing programs bigger than a single screen.

steps.title: Learn Python end to end
steps.summary: Python reads almost like English — the friendliest start.
steps.detail: Now put the building blocks together in a real language. Our Python course walks you from your first line of output through variables, control flow, functions, and working with collections of data — the same concepts above, applied hands-on.

steps.title: Write small programs
steps.summary: Automate a chore, build a calculator, parse a file.
steps.detail: Concepts stick when you use them. Build tiny, complete programs: a tip calculator, a number-guessing game, a script that renames files. Finishing small projects teaches you far more than reading ever will, and it builds the confidence to tackle bigger ones.

steps.title: Choose a direction
steps.summary: Frontend, backend, or computer-science fundamentals.
steps.detail: With the basics in hand, pick the path that excites you. Frontend is about what people see and click; backend is the servers and data behind the scenes; DSA is the computer-science core that powers both and most interviews. You can always explore more than one.

title: Frontend Developer
tagline: Build what people see and click.
description: The path to building modern, accessible web interfaces — from your first HTML tag to a working interactive application.

steps.title: How the web works
steps.summary: What happens between a URL and a rendered page.
steps.detail: When you open a site, your browser looks up the server's address, sends an HTTP request, and receives HTML, CSS, and JavaScript back. The browser then assembles those into the page you see. Understanding this request-response cycle early makes everything else — performance, debugging, APIs — click into place.

steps.title: HTML — structure
steps.summary: Mark up content with meaningful elements.
steps.detail: HTML describes what content is: headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images, forms. Using the right element for the job (semantic HTML) makes pages easier to style, easier for search engines to read, and usable by assistive technology. It is the skeleton every web page is built on.

steps.title: CSS — styling & layout
steps.summary: Control color, spacing, typography, and layout.
steps.detail: CSS controls how HTML looks: colors, fonts, spacing, and how boxes are arranged on the page. The modern layout tools — Flexbox for one-dimensional rows or columns, and Grid for two-dimensional layouts — are what you'll reach for constantly. Learn the box model first; most layout confusion traces back to it.

steps.title: Responsive design
steps.summary: Make layouts work on every screen size.
steps.detail: People visit on phones, tablets, and wide monitors. Responsive design uses flexible units and media queries so a single layout adapts gracefully instead of breaking. The reliable habit is mobile-first: design for the small screen, then progressively add space and columns as the viewport grows.

steps.title: Accessibility (a11y)
steps.summary: Build interfaces everyone can use.
steps.detail: Accessibility means your site works for people using keyboards, screen readers, or other assistive tools. Most of it is free if you start right: semantic HTML, meaningful alt text on images, sufficient color contrast, labels on form fields, and a sensible focus order. It's both the right thing to do and often a legal requirement.

steps.title: JavaScript essentials
steps.summary: Add behavior and interactivity to pages.
steps.detail: JavaScript is the language that runs in every browser and brings pages to life — responding to clicks, validating forms, updating content without a reload. Our course covers the core you'll use daily: variables, functions, arrays and objects, and how to work with them cleanly.

steps.title: The DOM & events
steps.summary: Read and change the page from JavaScript.
steps.detail: The browser exposes the page to JavaScript as the DOM — a live tree of elements you can read and modify. Combined with events (click, input, submit), this is how interactivity is built: listen for something the user does, then update the page in response.

steps.title: Fetch & talking to APIs
steps.summary: Load and send data without reloading the page.
steps.detail: Real apps exchange data with a server in the background. The fetch API sends HTTP requests from JavaScript and receives data — usually JSON — which you then render into the page. Understanding promises and async/await makes this asynchronous code readable instead of tangled.

steps.title: Version control with Git
steps.summary: Track changes and collaborate without losing work.
steps.detail: Git records snapshots of your project so you can review history, undo mistakes, and work alongside others without overwriting each other. Learn the everyday loop — stage, commit, branch, merge — and you'll never fear changing code again.

steps.title: Package managers & build tools
steps.summary: Install libraries and bundle your app.
steps.detail: Modern frontends pull in reusable libraries through a package manager (like npm) and use a build tool to bundle and optimize everything for the browser. You don't need to master configuration early — just understand what these tools do and how to add a dependency and run a build.

steps.title: Build & ship a real site
steps.summary: Combine everything into one project.
steps.detail: Pull your skills together into a complete project — a personal site, a small dashboard, a game. Shipping something real surfaces the gaps that tutorials hide and gives you a portfolio piece. This milestone matters more than any single topic above.

steps.title: Learn a framework: React
steps.summary: Component-based UIs that scale.
steps.detail: Once the fundamentals are solid, a component framework like React helps you build larger apps by composing reusable pieces and managing state predictably. Don't rush here — frameworks are far easier to learn well after you're comfortable with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

title: Backend Developer
tagline: Power apps from behind the scenes.
description: The path to building servers, APIs, and data layers — the engine room every application depends on.

steps.title: Pick a backend language
steps.summary: Start with Python for speed of learning.
steps.detail: Backends can be written in many languages; the concepts transfer between them. Python is an excellent first choice — clear syntax lets you focus on backend ideas rather than fighting the language. Our Python course gives you that foundation.

steps.title: Alternative: Java
steps.summary: A statically-typed, enterprise-grade option.
steps.detail: If you prefer (or need) a statically-typed language widely used in large companies and Android, Java is a strong path. Its type system catches whole classes of mistakes before the program runs. Take this instead of, or alongside, Python.

steps.title: Data structures you'll use
steps.summary: Lists, maps, and sets show up everywhere.
steps.detail: Backend code constantly organizes data in memory. Knowing when to reach for a list, a hash map, or a set — and roughly how fast each operation is — keeps your services responsive. You don't need the full DSA roadmap to start, but the basics pay off immediately.

steps.title: Databases & SQL
steps.summary: Store, query, and relate data reliably.
steps.detail: Most backends persist data in a relational database, and SQL is the language for working with it. Learn how to model data into tables, write queries that filter and join, and use indexes so those queries stay fast as data grows. Our SQL course covers the essentials.

steps.title: HTTP fundamentals
steps.summary: Requests, responses, methods, and status codes.
steps.detail: HTTP is the protocol the web speaks. Internalize the parts: methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) that signal intent, status codes that report outcomes, and headers that carry metadata. Every API you build or call is a conversation in HTTP.

steps.title: Build REST APIs
steps.summary: Expose your data and logic over HTTP.
steps.detail: A REST API maps resources to URLs and uses HTTP methods to read and change them, usually exchanging JSON. Learn to design clear endpoints, validate incoming data, and return consistent responses and errors. This is the core deliverable of most backend work.

steps.title: Authentication & authorization
steps.summary: Prove who a user is and what they may do.
steps.detail: Authentication answers 'who are you?' (login, sessions, tokens); authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do?' (roles, permissions). Always hash passwords, never store them in plain text, and check permissions on the server — never trust the client alone.

steps.title: Security basics
steps.summary: Defend against the most common attacks.
steps.detail: A handful of vulnerabilities cause most breaches: injection, broken access control, and leaking secrets among them. Validate and escape input, use parameterized queries, keep dependencies updated, and never commit credentials. Building this habit in early is far cheaper than retrofitting it.

steps.title: Testing
steps.summary: Catch regressions before users do.
steps.detail: Automated tests let you change code with confidence. Start with unit tests for individual functions and integration tests that exercise your API against a real database. A service with tests is one you can refactor and grow without fear.

steps.title: Build a real API
steps.summary: CRUD endpoints, a database, and auth.
steps.detail: Tie it together: build an API that creates, reads, updates, and deletes records in a database, protected by authentication. This milestone proves you can ship a backend, and it becomes a portfolio centerpiece.

steps.title: Deployment & DevOps basics
steps.summary: Get your service running in the cloud.
steps.detail: Eventually your code has to run somewhere other than your laptop. Learn the basics of packaging an app (containers), running it on a server, configuring environment variables and secrets, and watching logs. You don't need to be an expert — just able to ship.

steps.title: Caching & performance
steps.summary: Make slow things fast.
steps.detail: As traffic grows, performance matters. Add database indexes for common queries, cache expensive results, and avoid doing work you can skip. Measure before optimizing — guessing at bottlenecks wastes time.

title: DSA & Interview Prep
description: Data structures and algorithms underpin efficient software — and most technical interviews. Build the foundation here.

steps.title: Solid programming basics
steps.summary: Comfort with a language comes first.
steps.detail: You can't study data structures without fluency in some language. If you're not already comfortable writing loops, functions, and using arrays, start with our Python course, then come back. Python or Java both work well for DSA practice.

steps.title: Big-O & complexity
steps.summary: Reason about time and space cost.
steps.detail: Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory grows as the input grows. It's how you compare two approaches without a stopwatch — knowing that a linear scan is O(n) while a nested loop is O(n²) tells you which will survive large inputs. This vocabulary runs through every other topic here.

steps.title: Arrays & strings
steps.summary: The most common interview territory.
steps.detail: Arrays store items in contiguous, indexed slots; strings are arrays of characters. A huge share of problems live here, and two techniques unlock most of them: the two-pointer pattern and the sliding window. Get comfortable manipulating arrays in place.

steps.title: Linked lists, stacks & queues
steps.summary: Linear structures with different trade-offs.
steps.detail: Linked lists connect nodes by reference, making inserts and removals cheap but random access slow. Stacks (last-in-first-out) and queues (first-in-first-out) are simple but show up everywhere — undo history, task scheduling, breadth-first traversal. Know how each behaves and costs.

steps.title: Hash maps & sets
steps.summary: Near-instant lookup by key.
steps.detail: Hash maps store key-value pairs with average O(1) lookup, insertion, and deletion — which is why they're the single most useful tool for turning a slow O(n²) solution into a fast one. Sets are the same idea for membership tests. Reach for them whenever you find yourself searching repeatedly.

steps.title: Trees & graphs
steps.summary: Hierarchies and networks of data.
steps.detail: Trees model hierarchy (file systems, the DOM); graphs model arbitrary connections (maps, social networks). Learn traversal — depth-first and breadth-first search — and binary search trees. Our Core Data Structures course covers these in depth.

steps.title: Recursion
steps.summary: Solve a problem in terms of itself.
steps.detail: Recursion expresses a problem as a smaller version of the same problem plus a base case to stop. It's the natural way to walk trees and graphs and the foundation for divide-and-conquer algorithms. The trick is trusting the recursive call and getting the base case right.

steps.title: Sorting & searching
steps.summary: Classic algorithms and when to use them.
steps.detail: Know how the common sorts behave and that good general-purpose sorting is O(n log n). Most importantly, master binary search: on sorted data it finds an item in O(log n), and its pattern reappears in many problems that don't look like search at first. Our Algorithmic Thinking course builds this muscle.

steps.title: Dynamic programming
steps.summary: Break problems into overlapping subproblems.
steps.detail: Dynamic programming solves problems by combining answers to overlapping subproblems and caching them so each is computed once. It's the topic most people find hardest, so save it for last — but recognizing when a problem has optimal substructure is a powerful interview skill.

steps.title: Practice, practice, practice
steps.summary: Apply patterns until they feel routine.
steps.detail: Reading about algorithms isn't enough; you build intuition by solving many problems. Work through a steady mix of difficulties, and when you get stuck, study the solution and re-solve it later from scratch. Consistency beats cramming.
